Dinis's questions of 26 Oct 2026: can the decision engine contain skills that carry more than
they say; and an article just on the engine, with inputs, outputs, flows and diagrams.

hand-written SVG figures (architecture; the decision tree; the request and the verdict as JSON; a
skill under the engine). The engine as the context the prompt lacks; one request with no secret

a host under a ports-only policy asked); the architecture table (a hook with a local engine, a hook
with the organisation's service, sharness.bash: Setting, Setting well informed, Boundary); skills:
a policy shipped with the folder and bound to its hash, the effective rows as the intersection
with the session's, an action beyond them refused by name, the skill's measured delta as its
reputation, the narrowest default for a skill with no policy, and what the engine does not catch
(a secret in an allowed file, data on an allowed channel, words that change what is written, a
skill that rewrites the policy); the model explains and compares, never decides. Limits: no
engine or service exists; two prototype runs; the schemas drawn, not written; "documented cases"
is the editor's observation, none named or measured.

commits.body:
Dinis's question of 26 Oct 2026: have you written an article about the two stacks? Now yes.

/articles/two-stacks-on-tcp: one argument, in the newsroom's format, byline pbp@sharness. SHarness
is two stacks on TCP. The capability stack is the chain of doors and targets a request crosses at
runtime (the app, fs.s3, net.direct, the kernel, S3 or its twin), about 3.2 ms per mutual TLS hop
(24 Oct 2026), any hop on any machine in any language. The abstraction stack is the chain of
levels a policy descends once at launch (intent, profile, plain rows, doors and targets,
mechanisms, the ground), deterministic at every step so the hash of a sentence names the kernel
rules, nil cost at runtime. Both are hop chains under the mirror rule; both get abstraction and
distribution from TCP; they are two because capability and abstraction are different questions
and collapsing them gives either the unreadable manifest or a rules engine in the trusted path;
they meet at the one hash the person supplies. Each level can be run by a different party, which
is the enterprise control point with nothing in the request path. What it does not claim: nothing
built; deterministic expansion is a requirement, not a property; the 3.2 ms is one measurement.
The lead figure is a hand-written SVG of the two chains meeting at the hash.

The independent review of 26 Oct 2026 (two high, three medium, seven low), each fixed with a test:

- Rows: the vault-key shape ran in quadratic time on a long run of letters (measured 7.8 s on 80 KB),
  so one PUT of a megabyte of base64 pinned a door thread. Every shape is now anchored on a literal
  or a fixed field (the colon and the UUID first, then 20 run characters checked backwards), so the

  switched off by a row or a policy, and max_bytes can be lowered but never lifted (64 MiB hard cap).
- Door: the TLS handshake ran inside accept() on the single serving thread, so one idle TCP
  connection stalled every caller and a failed handshake was never audited. The listener stays
  plain; each connection sets its timeout and wraps itself in its own thread (TCP_NODELAY set), and a
  failed handshake lands in the audit as a connection error. The edge is checked before a byte of
  body is read, and the peer's role is read once.
- /v0/log is the launcher's to read; a caller sees only its own verdicts (the contract says so; the
  default session gains the launcher role; sharness-ai fs log uses it).
- Session.new refuses a non-empty directory that is not a session and chmods only the files it wrote

commits.subject: Review 1 of the door kit and sharness.fs: openat walks, decoded paths, capped twin, clean reasons, timeouts, key permissions

commits.body:
cli@'s own review of MVP 2 before security@'s, 26 Oct 2026. Fixed, each with a test:

- fs.disk: a directory component swapped for a symbolic link between the realpath check and the
  write could have led a write outside the root. Every path is now walked from the root with
  openat(2) and O_NOFOLLOW, writes and renames go by directory descriptor, O_EXCL temporary names;
  the check is the open, so there is nothing to swap. A link anywhere in the path is 403.
- fs: the URL path is decoded and stripped of ?query and #fragment before the within_root check
  (%2e%2e, ..%2f); paths over 1024 bytes and DEL refused; mkdir wants a string.
- fs.disk.twin: a cap (256 MiB) so a caller cannot grow the door without bound; ENOSPC as a disk.
- door: a 30 s socket timeout per connection; a Content-Length that is not a number is 400 rather
  than a traceback; every reason, row, peer, method and path in a verdict or audit line is one
  printable line of at most 300 characters (a caller's path is echoed, never a newline or escape).
